name: Puppy liner (tareme eyeliner)

lead: Puppy liner is an eyeliner technique in which the outer wing sweeps downward instead of up and out, creating the look of downturned, rounded eyes. The Japanese word tareme, meaning droopy eyes, is used for the same soft, gentle effect. People use it to make the eyes look larger, sweeter and more youthful.
Coverage describes it as an offshoot of TikTok looks called sad eyes and sleepy eyes, and as the counter-trend to upturned fox eyes. It is cosmetic and temporary, with no clinical research behind it.

paras: The wing is drawn downward from the outer corner along the line of the lower lashes, often in a short subtle version for daytime or a longer dramatic one. It is combined with lower-lash-line emphasis and soft shading. It takes a few minutes and washes off.

Risks are those of eye makeup generally, such as irritation from products near the eye. Commentators also note that eye-shape trends change quickly and can leave people feeling their natural shape is out of fashion [1].

lead: Puppy liner is an eyeliner style in which the winged line curves downward at the outer corner, producing the illusion of downturned eyes [1]. The look is also called tareme eyeliner, after the Japanese term for droopy, gentle-looking eyes.

People use it to make eyes appear rounder and softer, and it is often promoted for hooded or downturned eyes, for which an upward wing is harder to draw. Fashion coverage describes it as growing out of TikTok's sad-eyes and sleepy-eyes looks, which emphasise the lower lash line for a doll-like effect [1].

It followed the fox-eye trend, an upturned look that drew criticism for appropriating East Asian features [1]. Eyeliner itself has a long history, from kohl in ancient Egypt to the liquid winged liner of the 1960s [2].
infobox: Sad eyes, sleepy eyes; opposite of fox eyes[1]

paras: The technique is an inverted version of the cat-eye wing [1]. It rose through TikTok in the early 2020s, according to fashion-media coverage, as a reaction to the fox-eye look [1].

Highsnobiety's commentary argues that eye shape is largely genetic and that trend cycles around it can make people feel inadequate, and it expects the industry to market procedures aligned with each look [1].
